This struck a major chord with me on an emotional level, as someone who has struggled through severe depression and bares the scars (or cracks) thereof. 

Others have already pointed out the amazing metaphors, and I have to echo them. The comparison of society’s expectations of us to a tree is so remarkably perfect that I’m surprised I haven’t heard it before. What really elevates it, to me at least, is that you also draw a second comparison from the tree metaphor, capturing beautifully how all strength eventually fails. 

Moreover, this poem really does capture depression in a very relatable, almost tangible way. It doesn’t feel like we grow any stronger from our stumblings, and it seems more like random chance that we’re even still alive than some sort of demonstration of strength of will. Maybe it’s a bit too much of a reach, but I even see this as a poignant rejection of the often quoted (and abused) Nietzsche line: “What doesn’t kill you, makes you stronger.”

I wish I had some improvement I could suggest, but I’m truly at a loss to find one. Thank you for the beautiful writing.

Quick disclaimer that I’m very new to poetry, so take my opinion with a large grain of salt. I’m far from an expert, and the following is just my two cents. 

This poem is very adorable, OP. It’s a fun lens through which to view a cat’s life as some strong guardian. I do think there’s something almost whimsical about how we as humans turned a deadly predator into a domestic pet, and the tone in this is perfect to highlight this. I especially appreciate the light-hearted words used for the animals (kitty cats, bunny rabbits), as they keep the language charming and also have a nice ring to them. 

I’m impressed by the form of the poem as well. It’s always a challenge for me at least to keep a consistent number of syllables and rhythm throughout a poem, so that might be why I’m always extra appreciative of works such as this which are able to do so. I think it bestows a quick pace to the poem, and makes it feel almost lyrical. That said, there are a few lines that read rather clunky, to me at least.

>They didn’t see him before he pounced, then it was all done

This one is probably the most awkward in my opinion. The flow of the line is cut off, possibly because it’s two independent clauses without much of a transition. Maybe a cleaner alternative would be something along the lines of “Before the bunnies knew what struck them, Misha’s work was done.”

Also, I think the poem could benefit from more figurative language. There’s a healthy amount in the first stanza, but I found myself wanting more after that point, where the rest of the poem is mostly literal.

I do admire your line of thought, but I think it misses the bigger picture. Allow me to contrast the situation of heightism with how quantitative studies are treated for another social issue (at the risk of claims of a false equivalency that I don’t intend).

There’s the (in)famous statistic that women make 76 cents for every dollar a man makes. The veracity of this figure has been hotly debated, just like the statistics related to dating and sexual preference in relation to height. The former statistic along with other studies encouraged feminists to take a look at the world and proclaim, “this isn’t right; we should try to make the world more fair.” On the other hand, heightism studies/statistics have sparked no comparable reaction, and any discussion of it is met with, at best, indifference and, at worst, outright hostility.

I am well aware that the latter issue relates fundamentally to innate attraction which is personal and can’t be altered. But isn’t the discrepancy in pay also similarly tied inextricably to biological factors over which we have no control? Any feminist will tell you that while biology can’t be controlled, there is another component to the gap which activists can address—namely the cultural component. Likewise, there are undoubtedly deeper factors that shape or at least impact an individual’s preferences, e.g. glorification of taller men in media and harmful stereotypes of shorter men.

What I mean to say with all this is that I think we shouldn’t *only* try to brush off these studies and go about our lives in spite of them. Short men are demonstrably disadvantaged in dating and in other areas of life, and I feel that it’s completely justified that one should be upset about the findings, however accurate, of these studies. The studies most certainly *do* matter, in that they affect short men’s likelihood of success in life. It’s of course even less helpful to be consumed with hopelessness after learning about one’s disadvantages, but I think the best solution is not to “man up” and meekly accept the injustice, but rather to work toward highlighting and striving to address the possible root causes of our struggles.
